name: Letybo

angle.text: Users get Letybo to soften the frown lines between the eyebrows, giving a smoother, more relaxed look within days of the injection. It is one of several botulinum toxin brands in hardmaxx circles, and glabellar lines are the use it was approved and trialled for.

summary: A newer FDA-approved botulinum toxin for frown lines, also sold as Botulax in Korea.
note: Prescription-only; eyelid or brow drooping is among the reported effects.
currentQuick:
Letybo is a brand of letibotulinumtoxinA, a botulinum toxin type A injected by clinicians to soften frown lines. It was approved by the FDA for glabellar lines in February 2024.
Like other toxins it is temporary. It is discussed as one of several brands beyond the best-known names.
How it works: The toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, relaxing the injected muscle so overlying lines soften.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include headache, eyelid and brow drooping and eyelid twitching. Botulinum toxins are prescription-only and carry class warnings about spread of toxin effect.
deepLead:
Letybo is a brand of letibotulinumtoxinA, a botulinum toxin type A injectable. It is used to soften frown lines between the eyebrows (glabellar lines) and, in routine practice, in the upper face more broadly. The US Food and Drug Administration approved it for glabellar lines in February 2024, according to Wikipedia.
The same toxin is sold in Korea and other markets under the brand name Botulax. Wikipedia lists headache, drooping of the eyelid and brow, and eyelid twitching among its most common adverse effects.
Published research on its aesthetic use includes observational studies of upper-face treatment and a registered comparison with other toxins for forehead lines.

name: Relfydess

angle.text: Relfydess is a ready-to-use liquid toxin that people choose to smooth frown lines, with the visible softening appearing after the injection takes effect. Its frown-line use is backed by a Phase 3 trial; interest in the liquid format comes from not needing reconstitution.

summary: Galderma's ready-to-use liquid botulinum toxin for frown lines, supported by a Phase 3 trial.
note: Prescription-only injectable; limited independent literature so far.
currentQuick:
Relfydess is a liquid botulinum toxin A from Galderma that needs no reconstitution. It is aimed at frown lines.
Its Phase 3 READY-1 trial compared it with placebo in adults with moderate-to-severe glabellar lines.
How it works: Like other type A toxins, it weakens injected muscles by blocking nerve signals to them.
Risks and caveats: It is a prescription injectable. Trial safety findings were not reviewed here, and off-label uses appear only as case reports.
deepLead:
Relfydess (relabotulinumtoxinA) is a ready-to-use liquid botulinum toxin type A made by Galderma, developed with a technology the company calls PEARL to produce a complex-free formulation. Unlike freeze-dried toxins, it does not require reconstitution.
Its Phase 3 READY-1 trial enrolled adults with moderate-to-severe glabellar lines, randomized 3 to 1 to relabotulinumtoxinA or placebo over six months, and reported patient-assessed effectiveness and satisfaction. A published 2026 case report describes off-label use for Frey's syndrome.

name: Nabota

angle.text: Nabota, sold as Jeuveau in the US, is used to smooth frown lines and is also discussed for slimming the masseter muscle in the lower face. Wrinkle use has trial support; the jaw-slimming use is studied in smaller reports and is largely off-label.

summary: Daewoong's botulinum toxin, sold as Nabota in Korea and Jeuveau in the US, studied for wrinkles, masseters and spasticity.
note: Prescription-only; formulation and immunogenicity data have been called limited in reviews.
currentQuick:
Nabota is Daewoong's botulinum toxin type A. It appears abroad and in the US as Jeuveau and is used for frown lines, masseter slimming and other indications.
Trials include comparisons against Botox in spasticity and wrinkles.
How it works: It blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, weakening injected muscle temporarily.
Risks and caveats: Reviews note that repeated exposure to any foreign protein can provoke immune responses and that evidence on purity of newer formulations is limited. Toxins are prescription-only.
deepLead:
Nabota (prabotulinumtoxinA) is a botulinum toxin type A made by Daewoong Pharmaceutical of South Korea. The same toxin is marketed in the US as Jeuveau, sold by Evolus and manufactured by Daewoong, according to Wikipedia.
It has been studied in post-stroke spasticity, blepharospasm, glabellar and crow's feet lines, masseter hypertrophy and calf contouring, among others.
Reviews note that evidence on the purity and immunogenicity of newer toxin formulations such as Nabota is limited.

name: Botulax / Hutox / Meditoxin

angle.text: These Korean toxin brands are used abroad to smooth wrinkles and to slim the jaw by reducing masseter bulk, which is the draw for people seeking a narrower lower face. Trials mostly compare them with Botox for wrinkles; the masseter use has been studied in smaller datasets.

summary: Korean botulinum toxin brands used abroad for wrinkles and jaw slimming, with trials mostly against Botox.
note: Prescription-only; reviews call evidence on purity and immunogenicity limited.
currentQuick:
These are Korean botulinum toxin A brands. Botulax is letibotulinumtoxinA and Meditoxin comes from Medy-Tox. Trials compare them with Botox.
Hutox has no studies in the material reviewed.
How it works: Type A toxins block acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, relaxing injected muscle.
Risks and caveats: Reviews note that any foreign protein can provoke immune reactions and that data on newer formulations are limited. All are prescription injectables.
deepLead:
Botulax, Hutox and Meditoxin are botulinum toxin type A products from South Korean makers. Botulax contains letibotulinumtoxinA, and Meditoxin (also marketed as Neuronox) was developed by Medy-Tox. They are used for wrinkles and, in studies, for masseter hypertrophy, spasticity and blepharospasm.
A 2020 review states that clinical evidence on the purity and immunogenicity of Nabota, Meditoxin/Neuronox and Botulax is limited. Hutox is named in this entry but no studies of it were reviewed.

name: Trap Botox (Barbie Botox)

angle.text: Trap Botox is promoted to relax the trapezius so the neck looks longer and the shoulder line more slender. It is an off-label cosmetic use; a 2024 systematic review exists, but cosmetic outcome data for this specific look are thin and mostly anecdotal.

summary: Toxin injected into the trapezius to make the neck look longer; a 2024 systematic review exists, cosmetic data are thin.
note: Off-label; neck and shoulder muscle weakness is a general toxin concern.
currentQuick:
Trap Botox means injecting botulinum toxin into the trapezius so the neck looks longer and the shoulder slope softer. It went viral as "Barbie Botox".
A 2024 systematic review covers the trend.
How it works: The toxin weakens the injected muscle so it relaxes and reduces bulk over time.
Risks and caveats: It is an off-label use of a prescription product. Detailed outcome data were not reviewed.
deepLead:
Trap Botox, popularly called "Barbie Botox", is the injection of botulinum toxin into the trapezius muscle, aimed at relaxing the muscle so the neck appears longer and the shoulder line slimmer. It is an off-label cosmetic use of a toxin.
A 2024 systematic review in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery examined the trend. Trapezius injection has also been used in clinical settings such as chronic migraine and cervical dystonia protocols.

name: Juvederm Voluma

angle.text: Voluma is a firm hyaluronic acid filler used to add cheek and chin volume, giving visible lift and projection without surgery. Users describe it as a temporary stand-in for implants; the volume effect is covered by manufacturer-backed studies.

summary: Firm hyaluronic acid cheek and chin filler from Allergan; temporary volume with studies behind it, plus filler-class risks.
note: Filler complications can include vascular events; results are temporary.
currentQuick:
Voluma is a hyaluronic acid gel injected deep in the face to add volume, mainly in the cheeks, and later approved in the US for chin and temples.
Studies follow treated midface patients for up to two years and report improvement and satisfaction; the effect is temporary and reversible with hyaluronidase.
How it works: A cross-linked HA gel (Vycross) is placed deep, near bone, where it adds volume and lift to overlying tissue and slowly degrades over months.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include swelling, bruising, delayed nodules and, rarely, vascular complications. It is a prescription medical device administered by licensed professionals.
deepLead:
Juvéderm Voluma (marketed in the US as Juvéderm Voluma XC) is a cross-linked hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal filler made by Allergan Aesthetics, an AbbVie company. It is a 20 mg/mL gel built with the company's Vycross cross-linking technology and, in the XC version, contains 0.3% lidocaine.  It is designed for deep injection to restore or add volume, and is best known as a cheek and midface filler.
According to Grokipedia, the US FDA approved it for midface volume deficit in 2013, for chin augmentation in 2020 and for temple hollowing in 2024.  In looksmaxxing and aesthetics discussions it is commonly described as a high-lift filler for cheekbones and chin projection; it is a non-surgical, temporary, reversible alternative to implants and osteotomies.
Controlled and open-label studies have followed midface treatment for up to 24 months and report volume improvement and high patient satisfaction.  Reported adverse events include injection-site reactions and, less commonly, delayed-onset nodules; filler complications in general have also included vascular events.

name: Juvederm Volux

chain: Chin and jaw angle built out
angle.text: Volux is a firm hyaluronic acid gel placed in the chin and jawline to build out a stronger lower-third contour, visible once swelling settles. Published trials cover chin and jaw augmentation; comparisons with Voluma come largely from forum anecdote.

summary: Allergan's firm HA gel for chin and jawline, with published trials and little community data beyond anecdotes.
note: Prescription medical device; one case report describes sterile abscesses.
currentQuick:
Volux is a firm hyaluronic acid filler intended to build chin projection and jawline definition.
A controlled study followed chin treatment for 18 months and a trial in Chinese adults reported chin improvement. Forum posts are limited to individual accounts.
How it works: A cross-linked HA gel (Vycross) is injected near the chin or jaw to add volume and shape, then gradually degrades.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include soreness and, in case reports, sterile abscesses. Like other HA fillers it can be dissolved with hyaluronidase. It is administered by licensed clinicians.
deepLead:
Juvéderm Volux (VYC-25L; Volux XC in the US) is a cross-linked hyaluronic acid (HA) filler from Allergan, made with Vycross technology and positioned as a firm gel for the chin and jawline.  A 2020 study describes it as designed to restore and create facial volume, and expert consensus authors describe it as a first-in-class Vycross filler for chin and lower-third remodelling. 
Published trials in chin retrusion, including a randomized study with 18-month follow-up and a study in Chinese adults, report effectiveness for chin enhancement.  A US trial registered for jawline definition enrolled 206 participants.  In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a jawline and chin option.

name: Juvederm Volbella

chain: Fine HA gel adds soft volume
angle.text: Volbella is a low-concentration hyaluronic acid filler used for subtle lip definition and to soften the under-eye hollow, with the change visible straight away. Randomized trials support these uses; later reactions in the tear-trough area are reported in the literature.

summary: Allergan's fine HA filler for lips and under-eye hollows, backed by randomized trials, with reports of late reactions in the tear-trough area.
note: Delayed reactions reported in tear-trough and lip treatment.
currentQuick:
Volbella is a thin, low-concentration hyaluronic acid filler used for lip enhancement, perioral lines and under-eye hollows.
Trials of up to 12 months report improved lip fullness, and infraorbital studies have been run in the US and China.
How it works: A lightly cross-linked HA gel (Vycross) is placed superficially to add soft volume and smooth fine lines; it degrades over time.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include swelling and bruising; one retrospective report described recurrent delayed reactions in the tear-trough area and lips. It is a prescription device given by licensed clinicians.
deepLead:
Juvéderm Volbella (VYC-15L; Volbella XC with lidocaine) is a low-concentration cross-linked hyaluronic acid (HA) filler from Allergan, made with Vycross technology and used for fine lines and delicate areas, chiefly the lips and perioral region and the under-eye hollow (infraorbital) area. 
Randomized and open-label trials report improvement in lip fullness out to 12 months, and trials in infraorbital hollowing have been run in the US and China.  Reports of delayed reactions in the tear-trough area and lips have also been published.

name: Restylane Defyne / Lyft / Kysse

chain: HA gels add volume by area
angle.text: This Restylane family covers cheeks and midface (Lyft), smile lines and contour (Defyne) and lips (Kysse), so users pick a product by the feature they want to change. The results are visible on injection; randomized trials exist mainly for Lyft.

summary: Galderma's HA filler family for cheeks (Lyft), contour and lines (Defyne) and lips (Kysse), with randomized trials for Lyft.
note: Filler-class risks include rare vascular complications.
currentQuick:
Three Restylane gels: Lyft for cheeks and midface, Defyne for lines and contour, Kysse for lips.
Lyft has randomized trials in midface deficit; Defyne and Kysse have less published trial detail in the available literature.
How it works: Cross-linked HA gels of differing firmness and particle size add volume and support, then degrade gradually; hyaluronidase can dissolve them.
Risks and caveats: Typical effects are bruising and swelling; rarely, vascular occlusion. These are prescription devices injected by licensed clinicians.
deepLead:
Restylane Defyne, Restylane Lyft and Restylane Kysse are hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal fillers in the Restylane range made by Galderma, which acquired the original developer Q-Med in 2011 according to Grokipedia.  Lyft is a large-gel-particle product for cheeks and midface (and hands); Defyne is a flexible gel for smile lines and facial contouring; Kysse is for lip enhancement and perioral lines. 
Randomized trials report effectiveness of Lyft for midface volume deficit and nasolabial folds, and trials have examined jawline, chin and nose uses.  In looksmaxxing discussions these products are referred to as options for cheeks, chin, jawline and lips.

name: RHA fillers (Teoxane)

chain: Flexible HA gel moves with face
angle.text: RHA fillers are designed to stay natural in areas that move, so people use them around the mouth and lips and in under-eye hollows. The filled look is visible immediately; randomized perioral and under-eye trials support these uses.

summary: Teoxane's flexible HA gels built for moving areas like the mouth, with randomized perioral and under-eye trials.
note: Thin community discussion; a hypersensitivity case report exists.
currentQuick:
RHA fillers are hyaluronic acid gels designed to flex with facial movement, used around the mouth, lips and under eyes.
A 52-week randomized study reported benefit for dynamic perioral lines.
How it works: A cross-linked HA gel retaining long HA chains adds soft volume and stretches with expression; hyaluronidase dissolves it.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include swelling and bruising; hypersensitivity has been reported. Prescription device given by licensed clinicians.
deepLead:
RHA (Resilient Hyaluronic Acid) fillers are cross-linked hyaluronic acid (HA) products from the Swiss company Teoxane, marketed as Teosyal RHA outside the US and RHA Redensity in the US. They were developed to hold up in dynamic areas of the face that move with expression, such as around the mouth. 
Controlled trials report effectiveness of RHA Redensity for dynamic perioral lines, and trials have studied infraorbital hollows, lips and nasolabial folds.

name: Belotero Balance

chain: Soft cohesive HA integrates in skin
angle.text: Belotero Balance is a soft hyaluronic acid filler used for fine lines and for under-eye hollows, giving a smoother, brighter-looking area soon after injection. A 12-month randomized comparison exists; forum posters also discuss filler as a precursor or stand-in for surgery, which is anecdotal.

summary: Merz's soft, cohesive HA filler for fine lines and under-eye hollows, with a 12-month randomized comparison and modest forum chatter.
note: Studied for lines and hollows, not structural projection.
currentQuick:
Belotero Balance is a smooth hyaluronic acid filler used for fine lines, folds and the under-eye area.
A randomized split-face study followed treatment for 12 months, and trials cover several skin types.
How it works: A cohesive polydensified HA gel spreads evenly in the skin, adding subtle volume; it degrades over time and can be dissolved with hyaluronidase.
Risks and caveats: Filler complications reported across the category include bruising, nodules and rare vascular events. It is a prescription device given by licensed clinicians.
deepLead:
Belotero Balance is a hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal filler from Merz that uses cohesive polydensified matrix (CPM) technology, designed to integrate smoothly into the skin. It is used for fine lines and superficial areas such as nasolabial folds, and has been studied for the under-eye (infraorbital) hollow. 
Published studies include a split-face randomized comparison of three HA formulations for nasolabial folds with 12-month follow-up and trials in darker skin types and infraorbital hollows.

name: Ellansé (PCL filler)

angle.text: Ellanse is a collagen-stimulating filler promoted for longer-lasting facial volume, because the body lays down new collagen around its microspheres over time. Support comes from small prospective studies.

summary: A PCL microsphere collagen-stimulating filler marketed for longer-lasting facial volume, backed by small prospective studies.
note: Slowly degrading microspheres; delayed granulomas have been reported.
currentQuick:
Ellansé is an injectable filler made of tiny polycaprolactone (PCL) beads in a gel. It is used by injectors for nasolabial folds, volume loss in the face and hands, and sometimes for skin quality.
Published studies are mostly small prospective or retrospective series plus a randomized comparison between PCL products. Authors describe results lasting longer than many hyaluronic acid fillers.
How it works: The gel carrier gives immediate volume and is absorbed; the PCL microspheres remain and are said to prompt the body to produce new collagen around them while they slowly degrade.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse effects include swelling, bruising and, more rarely, delayed foreign-body reactions or granulomas that have required specialist management. Fillers are regulated as medical devices and availability varies by country.
deepLead:
Ellansé is a brand of injectable dermal filler whose active component is polycaprolactone (PCL), a biodegradable polyester, formulated as microspheres suspended in a carboxymethylcellulose gel carrier. It belongs to the class of collagen stimulators (biostimulators): rather than only adding volume itself, it is described as prompting the body to lay down new collagen around the microspheres.
Published uses include correction of nasolabial folds, volume augmentation of the face and hands, and improvement of skin quality when diluted and placed in the dermis. Clinical papers describe the effect as lasting longer than that of many hyaluronic acid fillers, with the microspheres degrading gradually over time. Evidence consists of prospective studies, a randomized comparison between PCL products, small biopsy and case-series studies, and expert recommendations.
Reported adverse effects include injection-site reactions, and rarer delayed events such as foreign-body reactions and granulomas, for which case reports and a treatment report using ultrasound guidance exist. The product appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion mainly as a long-lasting option within facial volumisation and contouring, alongside other fillers.

name: Aquamid / polyacrylamide filler

angle.text: Aquamid is a permanent polyacrylamide filler chosen by people who want lasting facial volume rather than repeat sessions. The volume is visible on injection and stays, with a five-year study behind it and late reactions documented in the literature.

summary: A permanent polyacrylamide hydrogel filler that does not absorb, with a five-year study behind it and documented late reactions.
note: Non-resorbable: late inflammatory nodules have been reported.
currentQuick:
Aquamid is a gel filler made of water and cross-linked polyacrylamide. Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers it is not meant to be absorbed, so it is classed as a permanent filler.
Published evidence includes a pilot study and a five-year prospective study of 251 patients, alongside reviews and complication reports.
How it works: The gel stays in place as a space-filling implant, and, as the review literature describes for permanent fillers, the body responds to it as a foreign material rather than breaking it down.[2]
Risks and caveats: Papers on permanent fillers describe foreign-body responses with inflammatory nodules, some appearing years after treatment, and complication reports specific to polyacrylamide injections. Because the material persists, correcting a problem can require more than waiting for it to fade. Regulatory status varies by country.
deepLead:
Aquamid is a brand of injectable polyacrylamide hydrogel (PAAG), a non-biodegradable water-based gel with a cross-linked polyacrylamide network, used for soft-tissue augmentation. Polyacrylamide hydrogels are classed among the permanent or non-resorbable fillers, in contrast with hyaluronic acid fillers, which the body gradually breaks down.
Published use includes facial soft-tissue augmentation, and a prospective multicenter study followed 251 patients for five years after facial treatment with Aquamid. Related polyacrylamide gels have also been studied as bulking agents for stress urinary incontinence in women. The same literature documents adverse reactions, including inflammatory nodules, some appearing years after injection, and complications that have led to published reports on management.
Because the material is not designed to be absorbed, authors of review articles describe the treatment as effectively long-term or permanent, with corresponding implications for correcting unwanted results. The product is discussed in aesthetic-surgery literature much more than in looksmaxxing communities, where permanent fillers are mentioned mainly in the context of cautionary or irreversible-procedure discussions.

name: Autologous fat transfer to face

angle.text: Fat transfer uses a person's own fat to restore facial volume or reshape contour, favoured by those who prefer their own tissue over manufactured fillers. Fat grafting is an established surgical technique; how much of the fat remains over time varies.

summary: Using your own harvested fat as a face filler; well-established surgical technique, with variable retention and rare serious complications.
note: Part of the fat may be reabsorbed; rare vascular complications including vision loss are described.
currentQuick:
Facial fat transfer takes fat from elsewhere on your body and places it in the face to restore volume or change contour. Surgeons use it in facelifts, for hollow areas, and in reconstructive cases.
Most published material is narrative reviews and surgeon-reported technique, with some small registered trials of stem-cell enriched fat and processing devices.
How it works: Fat is collected by liposuction, processed, and injected as small amounts into target areas. Some of it survives as living tissue and some is absorbed; newer microfat and nanofat methods use finer preparations, partly for skin quality.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include swelling, bruising, lumps or contour irregularities, donor-site issues and fat necrosis. Rare embolic events including blindness have been described, and Wikipedia reports these are more frequent with fat than with hyaluronic acid. Retention varies from person to person.
deepLead:
Autologous fat transfer to the face, also called facial fat grafting or lipofilling, is a surgical procedure in which a person's own fat is harvested from another part of the body, processed, and injected into the face to restore volume or alter contour. It is used for facial rejuvenation, where volume loss is recognised as a component of ageing, and for reconstructive and contouring purposes.
Reviews describe the technique as having evolved from simple grafting to smaller-particle microfat and adipose-derived stem cell (nanofat) injection methods. Plastic-surgery papers describe two long-standing concerns: that part of the transplanted fat is absorbed over time, and that lumps or bulges can form, particularly around the eyes. Possible benefits beyond volume, such as improved skin texture, are also discussed by some surgeons.
Unlike manufactured fillers, the material is the patient's own tissue, which proponents cite as an advantage; it requires a harvest site and is a surgical procedure, with associated risks. Wikipedia notes that embolic complications, including blindness, are more frequent with autologous fat than with hyaluronic acid fillers. The procedure appears in appearance-modification discussion as an option for restoring hollow areas such as the cheeks, temples and under-eye region, and as a component of full-face contouring.

name: Jawline filler

chain: HA or CaHA added along mandible
angle.text: Users get jawline filler to add definition to the jaw angle and chin and to soften the look of jowls, with a sharper line visible once swelling settles. It is a non-surgical route used by people weighing it against jaw surgery; trials are registered and the claimed value against surgery is opinion.

summary: Hyaluronic acid or CaHA injected along the mandible to sharpen the jawline without surgery; trials are registered but risks include rare vascular events.
note: Filler in the lower face carries rare vascular complications; effects are temporary and need repeat treatment.
currentQuick:
Jawline filler is a non-surgical treatment in which a clinician places a dermal filler, typically HA or CaHA, along the jaw to add definition or volume. It is often discussed as an alternative to jaw implants.
Several device studies for jawline contouring are registered, but the published literature mainly covers technique and risk.
How it works: The gel adds volume under the skin along the mandibular angle and border, changing the contour. It is gradually absorbed, so effects fade and repeat sessions are needed.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are swelling, bruising and pain. Reviews describe rarer events including contour irregularities, tissue necrosis, vascular occlusion and, in other facial areas, vision loss. A 2026 case report described occlusion of the sublingual artery after jawline filler. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.
deepLead:
Jawline filler refers to the injection of a dermal filler, most often a hyaluronic acid (HA) or calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA) product, along the mandible to add definition or volume to the jaw angle, jawline or chin area. It is a non-surgical option used to accentuate a sharper or wider lower face, to address a jawline contour deficit, and to reduce the look of jowls.
Registered clinical studies have examined fillers for jawline contouring, including a 180-participant study of a CaHA product, HA products from several manufacturers, and a study of filler in jowls. A 2026 review in Dermatologic Surgery groups jawline filler with temple, nose and lip treatment as high-impact but higher-risk areas, with possible complications ranging from contour irregularities to tissue necrosis, vision loss and embolic events.
In looksmaxxing communities, jawline filler is discussed as a reversible or lower-commitment alternative to jaw implants, and users on looksmax.org share before-and-after impressions and maintenance-cost estimates. Research on aesthetic-surgery interest finds that cosmetic procedure interest among men has changed over recent decades, which authors link to declining stigma.

name: Temple filler

angle.text: Temple filler is used to fill the hollow at the side of the forehead, giving the upper face a smoother outline and better balance. The fill is visible on injection; most published research on the area is anatomical rather than outcome-focused.

summary: Filler placed in the temple hollow to smooth the side of the forehead; common, but the area is anatomically risky and most research is anatomical.
note: Papers describe vascular occlusion and rare blindness risk; ultrasound guidance is being studied.
currentQuick:
Temple filler uses an injectable filler, usually hyaluronic acid, to fill the hollow at the side of the forehead that can appear with ageing or leanness. It is described as improving facial balance.
Most of the research is anatomical, such as vessel mapping, plus technique papers on safer injection planes. Registered trials mostly treat the temple as one of several areas.
How it works: The filler adds volume deep in the temporal fossa. Because arteries there connect with vessels supplying the eye, authors have studied ultrasound guidance and cadaver anatomy to place filler more precisely.
Risks and caveats: Papers list contour irregularities, vascular occlusion, skin necrosis, hair loss, blindness, stroke and non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism. Wikipedia reports blindness from retrograde embolization is rare but usually permanent. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.
deepLead:
Temple filler is the injection of a dermal filler, most commonly hyaluronic acid (HA), into the temporal fossa to restore volume in temporal hollowing, a concavity at the side of the forehead that is associated with ageing and facial thinness. Practitioners describe it as improving facial balance and, by softening the hollow, giving the upper face a smoother outline.
The temple is considered a technically demanding injection site. Papers describe temple volumisation as a very common minimally invasive facial procedure whose risks include contour irregularities, vascular occlusion, skin necrosis, hair loss, blindness, stroke and non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism. A substantial share of the published literature on temple filler is anatomical: cadaver imaging, vessel mapping, ultrasound guidance and injection-plane techniques aimed at reducing vascular complications.
Controlled clinical trials of filler specifically for the temple are limited; registered studies exist that include the temple among treated regions or combine it with other treatments.

name: Tear trough filler

angle.text: Tear trough filler is used to soften the shadowed hollow under the eyes, giving a more rested look quickly and with little downtime. Some people treat it as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery; the noticeable-yet-natural claim comes mainly from practitioner and forum reports.

summary: HA filler placed in the under-eye hollow as a subtle, quick alternative to eyelid surgery; delicate area with rare serious complications.
note: No standardised injection approach; delayed complications and rare orbital events reported.
currentQuick:
Tear trough filler uses hyaluronic acid injected under the eye to soften the hollow and shadow running from the inner corner of the eye across the cheek. It is promoted as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery.
Published evidence includes a 100-patient case series, systematic reviews of technique and complications, and several registered trials of HA products for infra-orbital hollows.
How it works: The gel adds volume along the tear trough groove, reducing the depth of the hollow and the shadow it casts. Injectors use either a needle or a blunt microcannula, and a review found no standardised preferred approach.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe side effects as generally mild and transient, such as swelling and bruising, while delayed complications can occur. A case report described orbital compartment syndrome. Wikipedia reports that blindness from filler embolization is rare but usually permanent. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.
deepLead:
Tear trough filler is the injection of a dermal filler, usually hyaluronic acid (HA), into the tear trough, the groove or hollow that runs from the inner corner of the eye diagonally down across the lower eyelid and upper cheek. Practitioners use it to soften the shadowed hollow and the tired appearance associated with infraorbital hollows, and some describe it as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery.
The tear trough is regarded as a technically demanding area. A 2022 systematic review of HA technique found no standardized evidence-based approach to injecting filler there, whether with a hypodermic needle or a microcannula, and a separate systematic review of delayed complications reported that side effects are generally mild and transient but that delayed complications can occur.
Published evidence includes case series, systematic reviews of technique and complications, and registered trials of HA products for infra-orbital hollows. In looksmaxxing forums, under-eye filler is discussed as a subtle correction with little visible change to the rest of the face, with users sharing cost and recovery impressions.

name: Cannula filler technique

chain: Filler placed through one entry point
angle.text: Cannula technique places filler through a blunt flexible tube instead of a needle, so users and injectors choose it for even spread of product across a wider area. It is a delivery method rather than a product; evidence is limited to small product-specific trials.

summary: Blunt-tip filler placement through a flexible tube instead of a sharp needle; only small product-specific trials exist.
note: Fillers carry rare but serious vascular risks regardless of tool; cannula-versus-needle comparisons are sparse.
currentQuick:
A cannula is a blunt, flexible tube used to place dermal filler under the skin in place of a sharp needle. It is used for areas such as nasolabial folds and the midface.
Published evidence specific to the cannula is thin: a few registered trials of individual products, without a broad comparison of safety against needles.
How it works: Filler is pushed through a rounded-tip tube inserted at one entry point and advanced through tissue, depositing product along the path.
Risks and caveats: Filler risks include bruising, swelling, infection, allergic reactions and, rarely, vascular embolization with vision loss or skin necrosis [1]. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.
deepLead:
The cannula filler technique is a method of placing injectable dermal filler through a blunt-tipped, flexible tube (a cannula) rather than a sharp needle. Practitioners typically make a single entry point in the skin and thread the cannula through the tissue to deposit product over a wider area. Fillers themselves are substances injected into skin or deeper tissue to smooth lines or add volume, and hyaluronic acid is the most common type .
Published human research on cannula delivery is limited to registered trials of specific products and devices. One completed phase 2 trial registered a metallic cannula against a standard needle for nasolabial fold augmentation , and a post-market study registered a hyaluronic acid product delivered by cannula for the same area . Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US and, with a CE mark, in the UK and European Economic Area .

name: Fraxel (Fraxel Restore / Dual)

chain: Smoother texture, less scarring and pigment
angle.text: Fraxel is used over multiple sessions to improve scars, sun damage and melasma, with the skin renewing over days to weeks. Small studies support these uses; Fraxel Dual adds a wavelength aimed at superficial pigment.

summary: The original branded fractional laser for scars, photodamage and melasma, with decent small-study support and a multi-session, several-day recovery.
note: Side effects documented include acne flares, herpes outbreaks and pigment change.
currentQuick:
Fraxel is a brand of fractional lasers that treat microscopic columns of skin, aiming to stimulate collagen and refresh texture, scars and pigmentation. It is performed in clinics in a series of sessions.
Published research consists mostly of small studies on scars, photodamage and melasma reporting improvement.
How it works: Laser energy absorbed by water in tissue creates microscopic thermal zones; surrounding intact skin speeds healing and the body remodels the injured zones with new collagen [1].
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include redness, swelling, peeling, acne flares, herpes outbreaks and, more rarely, scarring or pigment changes [3][9]. It is a medical-device procedure performed by clinicians.
deepLead:
Fraxel is a trademarked line of fractional laser systems for skin resurfacing, built on the principle of fractional photothermolysis: laser energy is delivered as an array of microscopic columns, leaving the skin between them untreated so that healing is faster than with full-surface lasers . Fraxel Restore and Fraxel Dual are non-ablative models using a 1550 nm erbium fiber laser, with the Dual adding a 1927 nm thulium wavelength for more superficial pigment targets .
Fractional laser resurfacing is used in aesthetic medicine for photodamage, wrinkles, acne and surgical scars, and pigmentation such as melasma . Published studies, mostly small clinical series, report improvement in these indications; a large series also catalogued side effects including acne flares and herpes outbreaks . Within looksmaxxing discussion it is categorised as a professional "hardmaxx" skin-quality procedure.

name: Clear + Brilliant

angle.text: Clear + Brilliant is a mild fractional laser people use as a starter or maintenance treatment for tone and texture, with minimal downtime. It is nicknamed a baby Fraxel and its support comes from small trials.

summary: A mild "starter" fractional laser for tone and texture with minimal downtime; backed by small trials only.
note: Evidence is small trials; many claims come from manufacturer-style descriptions.
currentQuick:
Clear + Brilliant is a gentle fractional laser used as an entry-level skin refresh for tone, texture and early aging signs, usually in a series of sessions.
Published support is limited to small studies.
How it works: Two wavelengths (1440 and 1927 nm) create tiny zones of thermal injury while leaving surrounding skin intact, prompting collagen remodeling and skin turnover [1].
Risks and caveats: Mild redness is reported to resolve quickly [1]. As a laser procedure it carries general fractional-laser risks, and results are described as lasting months.
deepLead:
Clear + Brilliant is a non-ablative fractional laser by Solta Medical, marketed as a gentle, low-downtime resurfacing option for early signs of aging, with an original 1440 nm handpiece and a 1927 nm Perméa handpiece . It is often described as a "baby Fraxel" and is positioned as preventive skin maintenance .
Published human data are limited to small trials: registered studies cover photoaging, periorbital rejuvenation and melasma in groups of 14 to 40 people . Claims of high satisfaction and millions of treatments come from manufacturer-oriented descriptions rather than from controlled trials .
